title: System Design & Software Architecture Explained ⚡ API Versioning
ig_caption:
System design & software architecture explained ⚡ API versioning—how to change without breaking old apps.
Why did every app crash after one rename?

• /v1 contract: returns full_name
• Client expects stable shape → YOUR API keeps “200 OK” *correctly*
• You rename full_name → “renamed”
• Without versioning, old clients deserialize wrong → boom

Under the hood:
• Version the API (e.g., /v1 vs /v2)
• Keep backward-compatible responses for a deprecation window
• Use explicit schemas + request/response validation
• Prefer additive changes; treat breaking changes as new versions

Practical takeaway: For system design interview questions, always call out compatibility guarantees + rollout strategy (dual-write/dual-read, canaries, deprecation).

Debate: Should you version by URL (/v1) or by headers/content negotiation—or is one approach always “best”?

API versioning is one of those “simple” backend concerns that decides whether your system is resilient or fragile.

What goes wrong (the classic crash-after-rename):
- Your API returns a response schema shape (e.g., /v1 returns full_name).
- A mobile/web client deserializes into its expected model.
- You rename a field (full_name → renamed) in a live endpoint.
- Even with HTTP 200 OK, clients can fail at runtime because the contract changed.

Core trade-offs and production patterns:
1) Versioning strategy
- URL versioning (/v1, /v2) is explicit, easy to reason about, and works well for system design interview questions.
- Header-based or content negotiation versioning can reduce URL clutter, but increases complexity and requires stronger governance.

2) Backward compatibility guarantees
- Additive changes: introduce new fields without removing/renaming old ones.
- Breaking changes: ship as a new version and keep the old one running for a deprecation window.

3) Governance mechanisms
- Schema validation (request/response) at the API boundary.
- Contract tests between frontend/mobile and backend.
- Observability: track error rates by client version and route/version usage.

4) Rollout approach
- Canary releases for new versions.
- Dual-stack (route both old and new) during migration.
- Publish migration notes and deadlines.

Practical takeaway: When explaining scalable backend architecture, emphasize the “contract” mindset—versioning isn’t about features, it’s about preserving interoperability.

yt_title: System Design & Software Architecture Explained: API Versioning #Shorts
yt_description:
System Design & Software Architecture Explained ⚡ API versioning: how to change your API without breaking old apps.

In this Short, we show why a simple rename can crash clients:
- /v1 returns: full_name
- You rename the field in-place
- Old clients deserialize wrong → failures even when status stays 200
- Solution: create /v2 with the new contract (e.g., name)

Key under-the-hood takeaways:
- Version your API (URL/header) for breaking changes
- Keep backward compatibility during a deprecation window
- Use explicit schemas + validation + contract tests
- Roll out safely (canary + observability by version)
